_comment: THE LAST CUSTOMER (GDD 26). Written 2026-08-12; NOT LOADED YET -- the parser lands in PLAN_last_call S1/S5. THE BAR OPENED THIS WEEK: nothing here may lean on the room having a past, because it does not have one. THE FIRST LAST CALL IS ECE'S: on night one she crosses the bar, sits, asks for a drink the well can already pour, and introduces the arc -- the beat teaches itself on a night nothing can be lost. Ece works the shift with the player, teaches (lessons) and frames each beat (hostBefore/hostAfter); the player owns the bar, which is the only version that does not fight the screens -- the till, the rent and the shopping are already theirs. GUESTS COME AT THE WEEKEND: a beat is scheduled as a WEEK plus a NIGHT of the bar's six-night calendar (Tuesday-Sunday, Mondays dark), and a guest's night must be friday or saturday -- refused at load otherwise. That is what makes the quiet nights the shopping nights: the ask names what is missing and the player has until the weekend to go and buy it. Only the house may work a quiet night, which is why Ece's beat zero is a Tuesday. A missed beat returns on ITS OWN night, 'returnsAfterWeeks' weeks later. Every 'recipe' is an id from recipes.json, every 'look' is a slug in papers.json, every 'needStyle' is a style the market sells. Names and lines are the author's to replace; the SHAPE is the design: the ask names what is missing, no beat is a dead end, two lines a beat and one sentence each.

characters.blurb: Works the shift with you. Has done this before, in rooms that did not make it. Takes the first last call herself.
Collects for the building. Never raises his voice, never has to.
Came in out of the rain on the second night and kept coming back.
Writes about rooms like this one. Orders the same drink everywhere, on purpose.

ask: Door is shut. Pour me one of whatever we actually have.
Owner's first night. It is a rule somewhere.
nudge: Anything on that shelf. I am not the difficult one.
servedRight: Not bad for a room that did not exist last week.
Soon they will ask for things we do not stock — say yes, then go and buy it.
servedWrong: That is not what I asked for, and I am the easy one.
declined: You are turning down the bartender. Bold.

ask: So you are the one who took it on.
A whiskey. Neat. I will wait while you look.
nudge: Still nothing brown on that shelf.
servedRight: The building can wait a week. Do not make me come back twice.
servedWrong: That is not whiskey, and we both know it.
declined: Then buy a bottle. I will come back.
hostBefore: That one is here about the building, not the whiskey.
hostAfter: He will be back. They always come back to see if you lasted.

ask: My brother used to make me a mule when the day had been long.
Ginger, lime, and the copper cup he never actually owned.
nudge: Still no ginger. He always said it was the cheap half of it.
servedRight: Close enough that I had to put it down for a second.
Keep the page. He would have liked that it is yours now.
declined: It is a small thing to stock. I will ask again.
hostBefore: She was here on the second night, in the rain. She stayed.
hostAfter: That is how a regular starts. One drink somebody remembers.

ask: A Manhattan. Stirred — I will know the difference.
Here is how it is built. Every room gets one honest paragraph; this is yours.
nudge: Vermouth. It is not an optional ingredient, it is half the drink.
servedRight: Stirred, cold, and not drowned. Good.
I will say the room is worth the walk.
servedWrong: You shook it. I can see the ice in it from here.
declined: An honest no is worth a paragraph too. Later, then.
hostBefore: I know that face. He wrote the room I worked in out of business.
hostAfter: One honest paragraph. That is more than most new rooms get.

say: Six bottles and a keg. That is a bar, technically.
Read them before you pour — the licence says what they came for.
Click the stool, not the drink.
Nobody tells you what they want until you ask.
Two spirits in one tin do not become a drink on their own.
Shake it or stir it. The book says which.
Beer is not a cocktail. Lean the glass, then straighten it.
The head is the whole job.
Whatever we did not stock tonight, somebody will ask for tomorrow.
Buy narrow. A wide shelf on a new bar is just money standing still.
We cannot pour that. Not tonight.
Tell them straight — they come back for straight.
That is one red night. Three and the room is somebody else's.
I have watched it happen twice. Not keen on a third.
